blocks.text: Esther does not present her request as merely a private danger: she identifies herself with a people marked for destruction. This scene can therefore be read as portraying group-directed hatred and an annihilating threat. Modern terms such as antisemitism and genocide may help name that pattern, but they should not simply be equated with ancient events or movements without further historical analysis.

Chapter 7 brings a reversal prepared in the preceding scene: after the king’s sleepless night led to Mordecai’s previously overlooked service being read and publicly honored, Haman is exposed at Esther’s second banquet and dies on the structure he had prepared for Mordecai. The narrative’s repeated reversals and sharp symmetry are among the features that have led readers to describe Esther in several ways—including as history, historical novella, comedy, court tale, or an account connected with a festival—without any one label settling every historical question.

Readers may encounter materially different forms of Esther. Greek versions expand and interpret the story through elements such as dreams, prayers, divine naming, and fuller documents; they are not simply the Hebrew narrative with a few added devotional comments. As a result, Jewish, Protestant, Catholic, and Orthodox readers may meet different canonical forms of the book.
